verdicts.quote: the length of a head, used to compare how tall people are or how close a race was
verdicts.reason: A head is a unit equal to the length of a human or animal head, but its use in a race means a very small winning distance; it is not normally used to compare people's height.

verdicts.quote: Ana is a head taller than her sister.
verdicts.reason: This is not an idiomatic way to compare people's height; a head is used chiefly as a distance in racing.

verdicts.quote: often before another noun
verdicts.reason: This sense also commonly occurs as a predicative complement without a following noun, as in “She is head of the school,” so the code is misleading.

verdicts.quote: Head teacher is British; the American word is principal.
verdicts.reason: Principal is chiefly the head of a school, while head teacher can also mean a senior teacher or school leader; the statement makes an overly broad and inaccurate equivalence.

verdicts.quote: Turn to the head of the page.
verdicts.reason: “The head of the page” is not a natural expression for the top of a page; “top of the page” is the normal wording.

verdicts.quote: at the head of the page
verdicts.reason: This is not a typical collocation for the top of a page; use “at the top of the page.”

verdicts.quote: the side of a coin with the picture of a person on it, called when a coin is thrown to decide something
verdicts.reason: Not all coins have a picture of a person; heads is conventionally the side bearing the principal design or face, and the definition wrongly makes coin tossing part of the meaning.

verdicts.quote: Heads is the side with the face on it.
verdicts.reason: This is not reliably true of coins, whose heads side may bear a national symbol or other principal design rather than a face.

verdicts.quote: Usually head over heels in love. Fall head over heels can also mean fall so that the body turns right over.
verdicts.reason: The second sentence is misleading: “fall head over heels” normally also means fall deeply in love; the physical sense is rare and normally expressed differently.

verdicts.quote: Most languages also use the body word for the mind, the leader, and the top
verdicts.reason: This is an unsupported universal claim and is unlikely to be true across languages; adaptation notes must be language-neutral and factually reliable.

verdicts.quote: the head of a company may be a director
verdicts.reason: A director is only one possible senior role and is not a dependable equivalent of “head of a company.”

verdicts.quote: Nodding the head means yes and shaking it from side to side means no in English-speaking countries
verdicts.reason: This is an overgeneralization about gesture meanings across all English-speaking countries and cultures.

verdicts.quote: the part of the body above the neck, where the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and brain are
verdicts.reason: A common current sense is missing: “a person who is mentally or emotionally stable or unstable,” as in “She is a good head” only? No.
